passage: On the rooftop of the boys' hostel in the small town, Yamini sat with Darshan after the first coding test results. Darshan had scored badly and looked at the floor. "Everyone else understands this. I am not made for it." Yamini was quiet, then said, "My first coding round I failed. I could not even write the loop. I told nobody for a week. I thought everyone in the room knew what I did not." Darshan looked up. "You did?" "I did. Then I sat with a senior who showed me how to trace one line at a time. It was slow, and then it wasn't." Darshan let out a long breath. The fear had not vanished, but it felt shared now.

qa.q: What did Yamini fail in the first coding round?
qa.a: Yamini could not even write the loop in the first coding round.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel after the low test score?
qa.a: Darshan felt ashamed and doubtful, and believed everyone else understood the work while Darshan was not made for it.

qa.q: What could Darshan try next, and why?
qa.a: Darshan could trace a program one line at a time with a senior, because Yamini found that slow method worked in the end.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel about telling the story of failing?
qa.a: Yamini probably felt a little exposed but hopeful that it would help, since sharing it made the fear seem common.

grounding: A mentor recalls failing a first coding round and tells the junior honestly to show that the fear is common and can be worked through.

passage:
In a café near the university in Ankara, Rafael, a first-year exchange student from Brazil, admitted he was thinking of skipping the internship coding test. 'Everyone else is better. I'll freeze and fail.'
Elif, his mentor, stirred her tea. She thought about giving him tips. Instead she decided to tell him the truth.
'In my second year I failed the first coding round at the company where I'm now interning. Completely. I solved zero out of three. I froze on the first question, panicked, and wasted forty minutes.'
Rafael stared. 'You? But you're...'
'I practised timed problems every week after that. I learned to skip a question I'm stuck on. I applied again the next year and passed.' She shrugged. 'That fear you have? I had it too. It's normal. It doesn't mean you'll fail. It means it matters to you.'
Rafael sat back. 'Okay. Maybe I'll take it. And practise with a timer first.'

qa.q: How many questions did Elif solve in her first coding round?
Why did Elif choose to share her failure instead of giving tips?
qa.a: She sensed Rafael's fear and wanted him to feel less alone, showing honestly that failing once is common and can be worked through.

qa.q: What could Elif suggest Rafael practise this week?
qa.a: Timed problems, plus the habit of skipping a question he is stuck on, as Elif did before passing.

qa.q: How does Rafael see Elif after hearing the story?
qa.a: Rafael is surprised, having assumed she was always good, and feels encouraged enough to take the test.

grounding: Shows a mentor honestly sharing a failed first coding round to show the junior that the fear is common and can be worked through.

subtype: Approach: analogy to own early struggles [Thinking]

Outside the placement cell, the queue for coding-test registration curled round the corridor. Pallavi stood at the back, form in hand, not moving forward.
Naveen, her senior mentor, spotted her from the notice board. 'You're registering?'
'I don't know. What if I blank? Everyone in my batch has been practising for months.'
Naveen leaned against the wall. He remembered his own second year too well. 'Can I tell you something embarrassing? In my first coding round, I didn't pass a single test case. I spent twenty minutes on a spelling mistake in my code. I went back to the hostel and didn't talk to anyone for a day.'
Pallavi looked up. 'Then what?'
'Then I started doing one timed problem every evening. Next round, I cleared it. The fear didn't go away. I just learned it wasn't a sign.'
Pallavi looked at the form, then stepped forward in the queue.

qa.q: What did Naveen spend twenty minutes on in his first round?
qa.a: A spelling mistake in his code.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling in the queue, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was afraid of blanking, which shows in her standing still at the back, form in hand, not moving forward.

qa.q: What small step could Pallavi take tonight?
qa.a: Do one timed problem, as Naveen did, to start getting used to the pressure.

qa.q: How might Naveen feel sharing an embarrassing memory?
qa.a: Naveen may feel a little exposed but glad, since his honesty helps Pallavi step forward.

grounding: Shows a mentor sharing an early failed coding round to show the junior that her fear is common and can be worked through.
